guideTitle: Best Leaf Blowers for Wet Leaves (2026)
metaTitle: Best Leaf Blowers for Wet Leaves in 2026
metaDescription: Six leaf blowers rated for wet, matted leaves, gas and cordless, compared by air speed, volume, weight and runtime so soggy piles actually move.
expertTake: The Husqvarna 360BT is the best wet-leaf blower because 232 MPH and 890 CFM on a real engine can peel and push a soggy mat that a battery blower can only nudge. The wrydao 780 CFM is the value cordless pick, at only 3 pounds. Skip the cheapest handheld jets entirely: wet leaves are heavy, and a weak blower will only smear them across the lawn.
introParagraphs: Wet leaves are the hardest job a leaf blower is asked to do. Water makes each leaf several times heavier, glues them into a mat and presses them flat against turf, so the blower must break the bond with speed and then carry the weight with volume.

That is why the figures on a spec sheet mean less than usual. A blower that handles dry leaves perfectly can stall on a soggy pile, and turbo modes that look generous on paper drain a battery in minutes. Endurance and honest numbers matter.

products.name: Husqvarna 360BT gas backpack, 65.6cc, 890 CFM, 232 MPH
products.description:
Wet leaves expose the difference between peak and sustained output, and a gas engine is the better bet for sustained. The 360BT's 65.6cc X-Torque two-stroke keeps the fan at speed for as long as there is fuel in the tank, so the jet that breaks the mat keeps coming. The 232 MPH tip speed is what peels leaves off turf, and 890 CFM carries their weight along.

The backpack harness is not just comfort. Wet work means more passes, and the weight of a gas engine on your hips is far more tolerable than the same weight in your wrist. Against the PROYAMA at 880 CFM, the Husqvarna matches on paper and wins on proven design and parts supply.

Wet leaf work is also hard on filters and plugs because debris and spray find their way in. Clean the air filter after each wet session, check the spark plug each season, and keep the premix fresh. A harness that has been soaked should be dried before storage. On a hill, work from the top down so gravity helps the mat move, and keep the throttle steady rather than pulsing it, since an engine that surges loses the jet speed you need at the leading edge.
products.bestFor: Heavy wet leaf loads where sustained output matters.
pros: 232 MPH jet breaks the grip of wet mats
Gas engine holds speed to the last drop of fuel
Padded harness for long, tiring passes
cons: Filters clog faster in wet work

products.name: EGO Power+ LB8803-2 cordless blower, 880 CFM, two 4.0Ah
products.description:
EGO's maker aims the turbo mode squarely at wet leaves and caked grass, and 880 CFM is the volume figure that carries wet weight. For a cordless tool it is the best attempt at a gas-class result without fuel, and the two 4.0Ah packs claim 90 minutes of work, though not at turbo.

The bind with wet leaves is that you will live on turbo, and turbo is a pack drainer. Expect the real runtime to be a fraction of the 90 minute claim. That makes a spare pack close to mandatory for a heavy wet job, and a good reason to buy into the platform if you already have EGO tools.

Store the packs indoors, let them cool before charging after a hard run, and keep the intake free of wet leaf fragments that can stick to the screen. A damp intake screen starves the motor and makes it hot. If you notice the tone of the fan change or the tool getting noticeably warm, stop for a few minutes rather than pushing on, because heat is what shortens pack and motor life in this kind of work.
products.bestFor: Cordless users who want the strongest battery blower for soggy piles.
pros: Packs shared across the EGO line
cons: Heavy handheld on long wet jobs

products.name: wrydao 21V brushless cordless blower, 780 CFM, 240 MPH, 3 lb
products.description:
The wrydao makes a surprising pairing: 240 MPH and 780 CFM from a tool that weighs only 3 pounds. That jet speed is what wet leaves need, and the light weight means you can hold it low and sweep for longer without arm fatigue. A six-speed lock dial lets you set a mid level and leave it.

The weakness is the batteries. Two 21V packs are a modest platform, and the 150 minute claim is a low-speed figure. In wet work you will be on the higher settings and the packs will run down faster. Against the EGO, it has less capacity and less platform backing.

Treat the lightness as the benefit it is. Keep the intake clean, and charge the packs after every job, since the six-speed dial and brushless motor are most useful when they have full power. With a tool this light you may be tempted to hold it one-handed, but wet work needs two hands on the grip so you can angle the nozzle under the mat.
products.bestFor: Smaller yards with wet leaves where light weight is important.
pros: 780 CFM and 240 MPH at only 3 pounds
Six speeds with a lock dial

products.name: NEO-TEC 52cc gas backpack blower, 564 CFM, 216 MPH, 18.7 lb
products.description:
NEO-TEC delivers 216 MPH, close to the Husqvarna's speed, from a 52cc engine in an 18.7 pound backpack. That makes it the lightest gas option here, and the maker claims it clears wet, matted leaves. An air purge system clears air from the carburetor and fuel lines so the engine starts with fewer pulls. A good starting habit on a damp morning is to prime fully, set the choke as directed and give the cord two or three controlled pulls rather than yanking repeatedly, which tires you before you begin.

The volume is the trade, at 564 CFM it moves far less air than the Husqvarna's 890 CFM, so a big wet pile takes more passes. On a half-acre with soggy leaves, that is fine. On two acres it will wear you out.

It is a lesser known brand, so check the parts and warranty terms. Practice the usual routine of fresh premix, clean air filter after wet work, spark plug each season and a drained tank before winter.
products.bestFor: Mid-size lots with wet leaves where a lighter gas backpack helps.
pros: 18.7 lb is light for a gas backpack

products.name: PROYAMA 72cc gas backpack, 880 CFM, 275 MPH, dual nozzle
products.description:
PROYAMA's pitch is the largest engine here, 72cc, plus 275 MPH, the highest air speed of any gas model in this guide. The dual-tube design gives you a flat nozzle to sweep wide and a round nozzle to concentrate the jet on stuck wet leaves, which is a useful pairing for a soggy lawn edge. Shock-absorbing straps and a balanced harness are described.

The tradeoff is the support behind it. The 3.7 horsepower is a claim, and the value tier hints at less certainty on parts and service. For a wet-leaf season, that matters less than a blower that starts reliably, so buy a service kit and keep a spare plug and filter.

Bolt torque is worth checking after the first few hours. Re-tighten the exterior fasteners, clean the filter after wet work, and drain the tank for winter storage. A harness that rubs at the hips is common on budget backpacks, so fit it over a close layer before the first long session and adjust the strap length.
products.bestFor: Wet leaves on large lots where a value gas backpack is acceptable.
pros: 275 MPH is the highest gas speed here
Dual nozzles for sweeping and concentrating
cons: Power claim is not an independent rating

products.name: PTBGLV 21V cordless blower, 600 CFM, 200 MPH, 2 x 6.0Ah
products.description:
PTBGLV matches 600 CFM with 200 MPH and two large 6.0Ah packs, and the maker is straightforward that 60 minutes is the low-speed figure. An axial-flow turbine fan moves a wide stream, while six speed settings let you drop the power for light dusting. For wet leaves you will be on the top settings, so expect much less.

The larger packs are the benefit: two 6.0Ah batteries hold more energy than the EGO's two 4.0Ah, though the tool has fewer features. It makes sense as a value cordless blower for a yard with a few wet-leaf days a year.

Because wet work is hard on cells, let each pack cool after use, store them indoors and keep the charger away from damp floors. Because the pair of large packs is the real value here, rotate them so each is used equally and neither sits discharged for weeks. Charge in a dry room and wait for the pack to cool before plugging in after a long wet job.
products.bestFor: Occasional wet-leaf cleanup on a mid-size yard.
cons: 60 minute claim is only on low
Weaker than gas on heavy wet mats

buyingCriteria.explanation: Wet leaves stick to turf by surface tension and need a fast jet to peel them loose. The Husqvarna 360BT at 232 MPH and the PROYAMA at 275 MPH are best at this, while a 150 MPH jet will skate across the top. Aim for at least 200 MPH.

Once peeled, the leaves must be pushed, and wet leaves weigh far more than dry ones. The EGO at 880 CFM and the Husqvarna at 890 CFM carry the load, while a 564 CFM NEO-TEC needs more passes. For heavy piles, 700 CFM or more is the useful threshold.

Turbo drains a battery in minutes, and wet work makes you live on turbo. A gas engine holds output until the tank is empty. For cordless, count spare packs: two 6.0Ah packs like the PTBGLV's are better than a claim of 90 minutes.

buyingCriteria.criterion: Weight over a long, hard job
buyingCriteria.explanation: Wet jobs take longer because leaves resist, so weight matters more. A 3 pound wrydao is easy on the arms, an 18.7 pound NEO-TEC backpack spreads the load, and an 880 CFM EGO handheld gets heavy fast. Match the carry method to the job length.
A round concentrator nozzle raises speed for stuck leaves and a flat nozzle sweeps a wide path. The PROYAMA's dual-tube design offers both. A single fixed nozzle forces a compromise.

Wet debris and spray clog filters and screens faster than dry work. A clogged filter lowers power on a gas engine, and a wet intake screen overheats a cordless motor. Plan to clean after every wet session.

howWeEvaluated.title: Peeling power
howWeEvaluated.description: We evaluated air speed first, from 200 MPH on the PTBGLV to 275 MPH on the PROYAMA. Wet leaves need a hard jet to release. Blowers under 200 MPH were marked down.

howWeEvaluated.title: Carrying capacity
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared CFM from 564 on the NEO-TEC to 890 on the Husqvarna. Volume decides how many passes a wet pile takes.

howWeEvaluated.title: Sustained output
howWeEvaluated.description: Based on the spec sheet, we treated gas as sustained and battery claims as low-speed best cases. Two-pack kits and larger Ah scored higher.

howWeEvaluated.title: Weight and carry
howWeEvaluated.description: We weighed the 3.0 lb wrydao against backpack models by job length. Heavy wet jobs favour harnesses.

howWeEvaluated.title: Care in wet work
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at filter, intake and harness exposure to moisture. Machines that are easy to clean scored higher.

howToChoose.subheading: Gas vs Cordless for Wet Leaves

cards.label: Gas
cards.text: The Husqvarna, PROYAMA and NEO-TEC keep speed all session and refuel in a minute. They are loud and need maintenance. They suit heavy, long wet jobs.

cards.label: Cordless
cards.text: The EGO, wrydao and PTBGLV are quiet and start instantly. Turbo drains packs and wet work lives on turbo. They suit light to moderate jobs with spares.

howToChoose.note: Gas for soaked piles and big lots; cordless for moderate dampness and smaller yards.

howToChoose.subheading: For Matted Leaves on Turf Specifically

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A jet above 200 MPH and 700 CFM or more behind it. Work in overlapping strokes with the nozzle low and angled under the leading edge of the mat, then push it downhill or toward a tarp.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Husqvarna 360BT and PROYAMA are the best for matted turf. The EGO LB8803-2 is the best cordless.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You face wet leaves every fall on a large lot. The Husqvarna's sustained output and proven support pay off over years.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: Wet days are rare. The PTBGLV 600 CFM or wrydao 780 CFM handles occasional damp work.

maintenance.why: Wet debris clogs filters and screens. A clean filter keeps gas engines at full power.
A soaked harness mildews and weakens stitching. Hang it to dry before storage.
Wet leaf fragments stick to the screen and starve the motor. A clean screen keeps airflow.
Let packs cool after a hard run and store them partly charged indoors.
Fresh premix and a clean plug prevent hard starts in damp weather.

faq.q: Can a leaf blower move wet leaves at all?
faq.a: Yes, but it takes speed and volume. A jet above 200 MPH peels leaves from turf and 700 CFM or more carries the weight. Weak blowers smear leaves instead of moving them.

faq.q: Gas or battery for wet leaves?
faq.a: Gas is the safer choice for soaked piles because output is sustained. Battery models work for moderate dampness with spare packs. Turbo drains cordless packs fast.
The PTBGLV and wrydao sit at the low tiers, the gas PROYAMA and NEO-TEC in the middle and the Husqvarna and EGO higher. Spend on speed and sustained output.

faq.q: Is it better to wait for leaves to dry?
faq.a: Yes, when you can. Dry leaves move far more easily and need less power. If you must work wet, run a higher setting in short bursts.

faq.q: Will wet leaves damage my blower?
faq.a: Wet debris clogs filters and screens, so clean them after each session. Avoid blowing into standing water. Routine care prevents problems.

faq.q: What is the best technique for wet leaves?
faq.a: Use overlapping strokes, keep the nozzle low and angled under the leading edge of the mat, and push downhill. Work in sections. A tarp helps.
